claim: NK cells eliminate disseminated tumor cells from the lung within 24 hr of arrival.
source: NK cells eliminated disseminated tumor cells from the lung within 24 hr of arrival, but not thereafter.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data showing rapid decrease in tumor cell numbers within 24 hours in control mice but not in NK cell-depleted mice (Figure 1).

claim: 50% of NK-tumor cell encounters lead to tumor cell death in the first 4 hr after tumor cell arrival.
source: Intravital dynamic imaging revealed that 50% of NK-tumor cell encounters lead to tumor cell death in the first 4 hr after tumor cell arrival, but after 24 hr of arrival, nearly 100% of the interactions result in the survival of the tumor cell.
evidence: Based on intravital imaging data showing Ca2+ influx in tumor cells after NK cell contact (Figure 4H).

claim: After 24 hr of tumor cell arrival, nearly 100% of NK-tumor cell interactions result in tumor cell survival.
source: Intravital dynamic imaging revealed that 50% of NK-tumor cell encounters lead to tumor cell death in the first 4 hr after tumor cell arrival, but after 24 hr of arrival, nearly 100% of the interactions result in the survival of the tumor cell.
evidence: Supported by data showing decreased Ca2+ influx in tumor cells after 24 hours (Figure 4H).

claim: The probability of ERK activation in NK cells upon encountering tumor cells decreases from 68% to 8% during the first 24 hours.
source: During this 24-hr period, the probability of ERK activation in NK cells upon encountering the tumor cells was decreased from 68% to 8%, which correlated with the loss of the activating ligand CD155/PVR/Necl5 from the tumor cell surface.
evidence: Based on FRET imaging data of ERK activity in NK cells at different time points (Figure 5E).

claim: The loss of CD155/PVR/Necl5 from the tumor cell surface correlates with decreased NK cell activation.
source: During this 24-hr period, the probability of ERK activation in NK cells upon encountering the tumor cells was decreased from 68% to 8%, which correlated with the loss of the activating ligand CD155/PVR/Necl5 from the tumor cell surface.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing decreased Necl5 expression on tumor cells at 24 hours (Figure 6A, B).

claim: More than 90% of NK cells in the mouse lung are in the vasculature.
source: Using a newly developed method of intravascular staining of immune cells (Anderson et al., 2014), it was shown that more than 90% of NK cells in the mouse lung are in the vasculature (Secklehner et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The major NK cell subset in the lung is similar to that in the peripheral blood.
source: In agreement with this finding, the major NK cell subset in the lung is similar to that in the peripheral blood (Hayakawa and Smyth, 2006; Marquardt et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NK cells in the normal lung have been proposed to be incompetent or hypofunctional.
source: Meanwhile, it has also been proposed that NK cells in the normal lung are incompetent or hypofunctional (Marquardt et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibition of platelets and coagulation factors has been associated with suppression of lung metastasis.
source: Inhibition of platelets and coagulation factors has long been associated with the suppression of lung metastasis (Brown, 1973; Gasic et al., 1968; Pearlstein et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Part of the pro-metastatic effect of the coagulation cascade is attributed to inhibition of NK cells.
source: At least a part of the pro-metastatic effect of the coagulation cascade is attributed to inhibition of NK cells (Gorelik et al., 1984; Nieswandt et al., 1999; Palumbo et al., 2005; Sadallah et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: αAGM1 antibody removes more than 97% of NK cells from the spleen and lung.
source: The pretreatment with αAGM1 removed more than 97% of NK cells from the spleen and the lung (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In control mice, bioluminescence signal decreased rapidly in the first 20 min, then gradually thereafter.
source: A bioluminescence signal in the control mice was observed almost exclusively in the lung and decreased rapidly in the first 20 min, then gradually thereafter.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in Figure 1A.

claim: In αAGM1-treated mice, the bioluminescence signal dropped rapidly but the decrease was substantially reduced after 20 min compared to control animals.
source: In the αAGM1-treated mice, the bioluminescence signal dropped rapidly as observed in the control mice; however, the decrease was substantially reduced after 20 min as compared to control animals.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in Figure 1A.

claim: In the initial phase (<180 min), there are at least two mechanisms that eliminate melanoma cells from the lung.
source: Thus, in the initial phase (<180 min), there are at least two mechanisms that eliminate melanoma cells from the lung.
evidence: Inferred from the biphasic elimination kinetics observed in bioluminescence imaging data.

claim: The rapid elimination of melanoma cells (<20 min) may reflect flushing away by blood flow or shear-stress-mediated cell death.
source: The rapid elimination of melanoma cells (<20 min) may reflect flushing away by the blood flow or shear-stress-mediated cell death.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the rapid initial decrease in bioluminescence signal.

claim: The slow component of melanoma elimination (>20 min) observed in control mice is caused primarily by NK cells.
source: The slow component of the elimination (>20 min) observed in the control mice is caused primarily by NK cells.
evidence: Supported by comparison of elimination kinetics between control and NK cell-depleted mice.

claim: In control mice, the bioluminescence signal of melanoma cells reached a nadir 24 hr after tumor cell injection and increased thereafter.
source: In the control mice, the bioluminescence signal of melanoma cells reached a nadir 24 hr after tumor cell injection and increased thereafter, indicating proliferation of melanoma cells.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in Figure 1B.

claim: In αAGM1-treated mice, the bioluminescence signal decreased very little after 4 hr and started increasing after 12 hr.
source: On the other hand, in the αAGM1-treated mice, the bioluminescence signal decreased very little after 4 hr and started increasing after 12 hr.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in Figure 1B.

claim: After 24 hr, there was no significant difference in the relative increase of bioluminescence signal between control and αAGM1-treated mice.
source: Importantly, after 24 hr, we did not observe any significant difference in the relative increase of the bioluminescence signal between the control and αAGM1-treated mice.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in Figure 1B.

claim: In both control and αAGM1-treated mice, the doubling time of melanoma cells is approximately 1 day.
source: In both mice, the doubling time of melanoma cells is approximately 1 day, implying that NK cells eliminate disseminated melanoma cells primarily in the acute phase (<24 hr) of lung metastasis.
evidence: Calculated from bioluminescence imaging data showing tumor growth kinetics.

claim: NK cells eliminate disseminated melanoma cells primarily in the acute phase (<24 hr) of lung metastasis.
source: In both mice, the doubling time of melanoma cells is approximately 1 day, implying that NK cells eliminate disseminated melanoma cells primarily in the acute phase (<24 hr) of lung metastasis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NK cell depletion affects tumor elimination only in the first 24 hours.

claim: NK cell-mediated elimination of metastatic melanoma cells operates in melanoma-burdened mice.
source: In this model, B16F10 melanoma cells continue to grow at the footpad until the day of B16-Akaluc cell injection. αAGM1 treatment hampered the rapid decrease of the bioluminescence signal, suggesting that NK cell-mediated elimination of metastatic melanoma cells operates in the melanoma-burdened mice as well.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in Figure 1C showing effect of NK cell depletion in tumor-bearing mice.

claim: The rapid decrease of bioluminescence signals in BrafV600E melanoma, MC-38, and 4T1 cells is markedly alleviated by αAGM1.
source: The rapid decrease of bioluminescence signals was markedly alleviated by αAGM1, supporting the critical role of NK cells in the acute phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Basophil depletion did not affect the elimination of melanoma cells.
source: The basophil depletion did not affect the elimination of melanoma cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data after basophil depletion.

claim: Monocyte depletion did not mitigate melanoma elimination within 24 hr of injection.
source: Neither treatment mitigated the melanoma elimination within 24 hr of injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–F).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data after monocyte depletion with clodronate liposome.

claim: Neutrophil depletion did not mitigate melanoma elimination within 24 hr of injection.
source: Neither treatment mitigated the melanoma elimination within 24 hr of injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–F).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data after neutrophil depletion with αLy-6G antibody.

claim: T cell immunity does not contribute to tumor cell reduction in the acute phase (<24 hr) in nude mice.
source: 4T1-Akaluc cells were eliminated in mice as efficiently as in wild-type (WT) mice in an NK cell-dependent manner, indicating that under these conditions, T cell immunity does not contribute to tumor cell reduction in the acute phase of rejection (<24 hr).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in nude mice (Figure 1D).

claim: αAGM1 treatment did not affect the growth of the primary tumor but suppressed lung metastasis.
source: The αAGM1 treatment did not affect the growth of the primary tumor, but suppressed lung metastasis (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging and metastasis counting data in Figure 1E and G.

claim: More than 95% of pulmonary NK cells are found in the vasculature.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Gasteiger et al., 2015; Secklehner et al., 2019), more than 95% of pulmonary NK cells (CD45+, CD3−, and NCR1+) were found in the vasculature, compared to 20% of bone marrow NK cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: NK cells flowing in the capillaries stalled on endothelial cells, crawled a short distance, and jumped back into the flow.
source: NK cells flowing in the capillaries stalled on endothelial cells, crawled a short distance, and jumped back into the flow (Figure 2C and Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data in Figure 2C.

claim: A histogram of NK cell crawling time exhibited exponential decay with a median of 2.5 min.
source: A histogram of the crawling time exhibited exponential decay with a median of 2.5 min (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of intravital imaging data in Figure 2D.

claim: Intravenous injection of αLFA-1α antibody resulted in a reduction of NK cells on pulmonary endothelial cells.
source: Intravenous injection of the blocking antibody against LFA-1α (αLFA-1α) resulted in a reduction of NK cells on the pulmonary endothelial cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data in Figure 2E.

claim: αLFA-1α, but not αMac-1, markedly reduced the number of NK cells on pulmonary endothelial cells.
source: As expected, αLFA-1α, but not αMac-1, markedly reduced the number of NK cells on the pulmonary endothelial cells (Figure 2F), indicating that the adhesion of NK cells to the pulmonary endothelial cells is mediated at least partially by LFA-1.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of NK cell numbers after antibody treatment in Figure 2F.

claim: The adhesion of NK cells to pulmonary endothelial cells is mediated at least partially by LFA-1.
source: As expected, αLFA-1α, but not αMac-1, markedly reduced the number of NK cells on the pulmonary endothelial cells (Figure 2F), indicating that the adhesion of NK cells to the pulmonary endothelial cells is mediated at least partially by LFA-1.
evidence: Inferred from the effect of LFA-1α blocking antibody on NK cell adhesion.

claim: The migration mode of NK cells can be classified as sub-diffusive with α<1.
source: Curves fitted with the measured data represent α<1 regardless of the presence of tumor cells, α=0.56 in the presence and α=0.53 in the absence, indicating that the migration mode of NK cells can be classified as sub-diffusive.
evidence: Supported by mean square displacement analysis of NK cell trajectories in Figure 3D.

claim: The displacement from the original position is smaller in the presence than in the absence of tumor cells.
source: MSD analysis also shows that the displacement from the original position is smaller in the presence than in the absence of tumor cells.
evidence: Supported by mean square displacement analysis in Figure 3D.

claim: The mean instantaneous speed of crawling NK cells was significantly decelerated in the presence of tumor cells, from 7.8 to 4.8 μm/min.
source: This observation is consistent with our present finding that the mean instantaneous speed of the crawling NK cells was significantly decelerated in the presence of tumor cells, from 7.8 to 4.8 μm/min (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of NK cell speed in Figure 3E.

claim: The median duration time of NK cell crawling was markedly increased in the presence of tumor cells, from 5 to 30 min.
source: In accordance with this observation, the median duration time of crawling was markedly increased in the presence of tumor cells, from 5 to 30 min (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of crawling duration in Figure 3F.

claim: The dissemination of tumor cells causes global activation of pulmonary endothelial cells, leading to slower crawling of NK cells.
source: Notably, these data exclude regions in which the tumor cells would physically block NK movement in the capillary, suggesting that the dissemination of tumor cells causes global activation of pulmonary endothelial cells, and thereby causes slower crawling of NK cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NK cells slow down even in regions without physical obstruction by tumor cells.

claim: A tumor cell lodged in a pulmonary capillary will be contacted by flowing NK cells roughly every 10 min.
source: In short, a tumor cell lodged in a pulmonary capillary will be contacted by the flowing and crawling NK cells roughly every 10 min and every 2 hr, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from quantitative imaging data and physiological parameters in Table 1.

claim: A tumor cell lodged in a pulmonary capillary will be contacted by crawling NK cells roughly every 2 hr.
source: In short, a tumor cell lodged in a pulmonary capillary will be contacted by the flowing and crawling NK cells roughly every 10 min and every 2 hr, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from quantitative imaging data and physiological parameters in Table 1.

claim: Caspase-3 was activated 16 min after an NK cell came into contact with a B16-SCAT3 tumor cell.
source: For the typical B16-SCAT3 cells, caspase-3 was activated 16 min after an NK cell came into contact with the tumor cell (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data of caspase-3 activity in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Caspase-3 activation was observed in 18% of contact events within a median of 26 min after contact.
source: The caspase-3 activation was observed in 18% of contact events within a median of 26 min after the contact (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of caspase-3 activation events in Figure 4C and D.

claim: 98% of cells that exhibited Ca2+ influx died by apoptosis with blebbing.
source: A surge of Ca2+ influx was observed only in cells that were doomed to die (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4—video 2); 98% of cells that exhibited Ca2+ influx died by apoptosis with blebbing (Figure S5D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ca2+ influx was induced within 3 min when an NK cell contacted a B16-GCaMP cell.
source: In a typical example (Figure 4E and F and Figure 4—video 3), when an NK cell contacted a B16F10 cell expressing GCaMP6s (B16-GCaMP), Ca2+ influx was induced within 3 min.
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Ca2+ influx was observed with a median lag of 6 min in 47% of contact events.
source: The Ca2+ influx was observed with a median lag of 6 min (Figure 4G) in 47% of contact events (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of Ca2+ influx events in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Tumor Ca2+ influx was almost completely abolished in Necl5−/− Nectin2−/− B16F10 cells.
source: As anticipated, tumor Ca2+ influx was almost completely abolished in the Necl5−/− Nectin2−/− B16F10 cells (Figure 4H), suggesting that damage to tumor cells is dependent on the engagement of Necl5 and/or Nectin2 on melanoma cells.
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data comparing wild-type and knockout cells in Figure 4H.

claim: Damage to tumor cells is dependent on the engagement of Necl5 and/or Nectin2 on melanoma cells.
source: As anticipated, tumor Ca2+ influx was almost completely abolished in the Necl5−/− Nectin2−/− B16F10 cells (Figure 4H), suggesting that damage to tumor cells is dependent on the engagement of Necl5 and/or Nectin2 on melanoma cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that knockout of Necl5 and Nectin2 abolishes Ca2+ influx.

claim: Crawling NK cells accounted for 77% of Ca2+ influx events in melanoma cells.
source: Crawling NK cells accounted for 77% of Ca2+ influx events in the melanoma cells (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by classification of NK cell types inducing Ca2+ influx in Figure 4I.

claim: αLFA-1α markedly attenuated melanoma elimination within 24 hr and after 10 days.
source: This markedly attenuated the melanoma elimination not only within 24 hr, but also after 10 days (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging and metastasis counting data in Figure 4J and K.

claim: LFA-1 is required for the crawling of NK cells on endothelial cells and for immune surveillance against metastatic tumor cells.
source: Our finding suggests that LFA-1 is required for the crawling of NK cells on the endothelial cells, and, thereby, for the immune surveillance against metastatic tumor cells.
evidence: Inferred from the effect of LFA-1 blocking on NK cell crawling and tumor elimination.

claim: Engagement of LFA-1 or DNAM-1 with their ligands results in the activation of ERK.
source: To track tumor cell induction of NK cell activation, a key step in the killing process, we took advantage of evidence that engagement of LFA-1 or DNAM-1 with their ligands results in the activation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) (Perez et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a positive correlation between ERK activation in NK cells and apoptosis in tumor cells.
source: Quantification of ERK activity in each NK cell during contact with the tumor cells demonstrated a positive correlation between ERK activation in NK cells and apoptosis in tumor cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Apoptosis was induced in 47% of tumor cells that were in contact with ERK-activated NK cells.
source: Apoptosis was induced in 47% of tumor cells that were in contact with the ERK-activated NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Apoptosis was never observed in tumor cells in contact with NK cells that failed to exhibit ERK activation.
source: On the other hand, apoptosis was never observed in the tumor cells in contact with the NK cells that failed to exhibit ERK activation.
evidence: Supported by in vitro imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MEK inhibitor PD0325901 suppressed NK cell-mediated apoptosis.
source: In agreement with this observation, an inhibitor for MAPK/ERK kinase PD0325901, called MEKi hereafter, suppressed NK cell-mediated apoptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro imaging data with MEK inhibitor in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ERK was activated more potently in DNAM-1+ NK cells than in DNAM-1− NK cells.
source: When NK cells were sorted into DNAM-1+ and DNAM-1−, ERK was activated more potently in DNAM-1+ NK cells than in DNAM-1− NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro imaging data comparing DNAM-1+ and DNAM-1− NK cells in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ERK was not activated in NK cells when B16F10 cells deficient in DNAM-1 ligands were used.
source: In line with this observation, ERK was not activated in NK cells when B16F10 cells deficient from DNAM-1 ligands were used (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by in vitro imaging data with Necl5−/− Nectin2−/− cells in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: IL2-stimulated NK cells poorly recognize Necl5 and Nectin2-deficient B16F10 cells in vitro.
source: Previously, Du et al., 2018 reported that IL2-stimulated NK cells poorly recognize Necl5 and Nectin2-deficient B16F10 cells in vitro (Du et al., 2018). We confirmed this observation with three independent clones of Necl5−/− Nectin2−/− B16F10 cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study and confirmed by in vitro data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: MEKi significantly attenuated the rapid decrease of injected tumor cell number within 24 hr.
source: MEKi significantly attenuated the rapid decrease of the injected tumor cell number within 24 hr (Figure 5A) and the number of lung colonies of MEKi-treated mice was significantly greater than in control mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging and metastasis counting data in Figure 5A and B.

claim: MEKi had no additive effect in αAGM1-treated mice in the early (<24 hr) time courses.
source: At the same time, we observed that MEKi had no additive effect in αAGM1-treated mice in the early (<24 hr) time courses (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in Figure 5A.

claim: ERK was activated 2.5 min after an NK cell's contact with a melanoma cell, followed by Ca2+ influx at 5.5 min and cell death at 10 min.
source: In a representative example, ERK was activated 2.5 min after an NK cell's contact with a melanoma cell (Figure 5C, upper panel; Figure 5D, magenta), followed by Ca2+ influx in the melanoma cells at 5.5 min and cell death at 10 min (Figure 5C, lower panel; Figure 5D, green).
evidence: Supported by simultaneous imaging of ERK activity and Ca2+ influx in Figure 5C and D.

claim: ERK activation was observed within 3 min in 60 NK cells during 88 contact events.
source: ERK activation, defined by a more than 30% increase in the FRET/CFP ratio, was observed within 3 min in 60 NK cells during 88 contact events (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A; Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of ERK activation events in Figure 5E.

claim: Ca2+ influx was observed at a median of 4 min in 43 of the 60 tumor cells that came into contact with NK cells having ERK activation.
source: Ca2+ influx was observed at a median of 4 min in 43 of the 60 tumor cells that came into contact with the NK cell having ERK activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B; Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of Ca2+ influx timing in Figure 5F.

claim: Ca2+ influx was not observed in 28 tumor cells that were touched by NK cells that failed to show evidence of ERK activation.
source: We did not observe Ca2+ influx in 28 tumor cells that were touched by the NK cells that failed to show evidence of ERK activation.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of Ca2+ influx events in Figure 5F.

claim: ERK activation in NK cells contributes to the induction of apoptosis in target tumor cells.
source: This result supports the notion that ERK activation in NK cells contributes to the induction of apoptosis in the target tumor cells.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between ERK activation and Ca2+ influx/apoptosis.

claim: 24 hr after injection, the probability of ERK activation and Ca2+ influx was markedly decreased.
source: Importantly, 24 hr after injection, the probability of ERK activation and Ca2+ influx was markedly decreased, indicating NK cells lose the capacity to activate in response to capillary-lodged tumor cells (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of ERK activation and Ca2+ influx at different time points in Figure 5E and F.

claim: NK cells lose the capacity to activate in response to capillary-lodged tumor cells after 24 hours.
source: Importantly, 24 hr after injection, the probability of ERK activation and Ca2+ influx was markedly decreased, indicating NK cells lose the capacity to activate in response to capillary-lodged tumor cells (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Inferred from the decreased probability of ERK activation and Ca2+ influx at 24 hours.

claim: 2.4 million NK cells in the lung outnumber 0.5 million melanoma cells injected into circulation.
source: Our quantitative data shows that 2.4 million NK cells in the lung outnumber 0.5 million melanoma cells injected into circulation (Table 1).
evidence: Calculated from quantitative imaging data and physiological parameters in Table 1.

claim: Pre-injected B16F10 cells did not affect the time course of clearance of B16-Akaluc cells.
source: We did not observe any effect of the pre-injected B16F10 cells on the time course of clearance of the B16-Akaluc cells, indicating that NK cells do not lose tumoricidal activity, but that over time, the tumor cells acquire the capacity to evade NK cell surveillance.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in Figure 5G.

claim: NK cells do not lose tumoricidal activity, but tumor cells acquire the capacity to evade NK cell surveillance over time.
source: We did not observe any effect of the pre-injected B16F10 cells on the time course of clearance of the B16-Akaluc cells, indicating that NK cells do not lose tumoricidal activity, but that over time, the tumor cells acquire the capacity to evade NK cell surveillance.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pre-injection of tumor cells does not affect NK cell function.

claim: Cell surface expression of Necl5 was markedly decreased in tumor cells isolated from the lungs 24 hr after injection.
source: As anticipated, cell surface expression of Necl5 was markedly decreased in tumor cells isolated from the lungs 24 hr after injection (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The ratio of extracellular mScarlet versus intracellular mNeonGreen was markedly reduced in 24 hr, indicating loss of extracellular domain.
source: The ratio of extracellular mScarlet versus intracellular mNeonGreen was markedly reduced in 24 hr, indicating loss of extracellular domain, possibly by cleavage or shedding (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data of Necl5-ScNeo fusion protein in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Warfarin potently accelerated the acute elimination of tumor cells.
source: Warfarin, an anti-vitamin K drug, potently accelerated the acute elimination of tumor cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data with warfarin treatment in Figure 6F.

claim: Edoxaban and dabigatran etexilate promoted the elimination of tumor cells.
source: Similarly, specific inhibitors of factor Xa and thrombin, edoxaban, and dabigatran etexilate, respectively, also promoted the elimination of tumor cells (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data with anticoagulant treatment in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Dabigatran etexilate did not have significant effect in αAGM1-treated mice.
source: Notably, dabigatran etexilate did not have significant effect in αAGM1-treated mice (Figure 6H), indicating that the anti-metastatic effect is mediated by NK cells.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data in Figure 6H.

claim: The anti-metastatic effect of dabigatran etexilate is mediated by NK cells.
source: Notably, dabigatran etexilate did not have significant effect in αAGM1-treated mice (Figure 6H), indicating that the anti-metastatic effect is mediated by NK cells.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect in NK cell-depleted mice.

claim: Thrombin cleaved off the extracellular domain of Necl5 from tumor cells in vitro.
source: In agreement with these functional results, thrombin cleaved off the extracellular domain of Necl5 from tumor cells in vitro (Figure 6I), and dabigatran etexilate suppressed the cleavage of mScarlet-tagged Necl5 in vivo (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data of Necl5 expression after thrombin treatment in Figure 6I.

claim: Dabigatran etexilate suppressed the cleavage of mScarlet-tagged Necl5 in vivo.
source: In agreement with these functional results, thrombin cleaved off the extracellular domain of Necl5 from tumor cells in vitro (Figure 6I), and dabigatran etexilate suppressed the cleavage of mScarlet-tagged Necl5 in vivo (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data of Necl5-ScNeo with dabigatran treatment in Figure 6J.

claim: Mice treated with edoxaban eliminated tumor cells almost completely.
source: The mice treated with edoxaban eliminated tumor cells almost completely, supporting the idea that the suppression of Necl5 cleavage promotes the elimination of disseminated tumor cells by NK cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by metastasis counting data with edoxaban treatment in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Suppression of Necl5 cleavage promotes the elimination of disseminated tumor cells by NK cells.
source: The mice treated with edoxaban eliminated tumor cells almost completely, supporting the idea that the suppression of Necl5 cleavage promotes the elimination of disseminated tumor cells by NK cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the effect of anticoagulants on tumor elimination and Necl5 shedding.

claim: Microthrombi around disseminated tumor cells were rarely observed.
source: However, we rarely observed microthrombi around the disseminated tumor cells, even when a microthrombus was easily induced by laser ablation in the vicinity of the tumor cell (Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Platelets may play a pro-metastatic role by promoting thrombin activation and thereby Necl5 shedding from metastatic tumor cells.
source: Considering the role of platelets as the platform for coagulation factors, platelets may play a pro-metastatic role by promoting thrombin activation and thereby Necl5 shedding from the metastatic tumor cells.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the role of platelets in coagulation and the effect of anticoagulants.

claim: The principal role of NK cells in the prevention of lung metastasis is to destroy tumor cells shortly after their arrival and lodging in the pulmonary vasculature, but not thereafter.
source: Our results demonstrate that the principal role of NK cells in the prevention of lung metastasis is to destroy tumor cells shortly after their arrival and lodging in the pulmonary vasculature, but not thereafter.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NK cells eliminate tumor cells within 24 hours but not after.

claim: Depletion of myeloid lineage cells did not affect the development of metastasis in the models employed.
source: However, depletion of myeloid lineage cells did not affect the development of metastasis in the models we employed (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), excluding a role of the myeloid cells in the clearance of disseminated tumor cells in the immediate-early phase.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data after myeloid cell depletion in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The rapid elimination of disseminated tumor cells within 24 hr is dependent primarily on NK cells.
source: Thus, the rapid elimination of the disseminated tumor cells within 24 hr is dependent primarily on NK cells in our models.
evidence: Inferred from the effect of NK cell depletion and lack of effect of other immune cell depletions.

claim: Pulmonary NK cells can eliminate disseminated tumor cells as efficiently as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells.
source: The crawling NK cells induce pre-apoptotic calcium influx in approximately 50% of the tumor cells that they contact (Figures 4H and 6K), indicating that pulmonary NK cells can eliminate the disseminated tumor cells as efficiently as do chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells (Cazaux et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from the efficiency of tumor cell killing and comparison to CAR T cells from cited study.

claim: Most of the tumor cells were killed by NK cells crawling on the pulmonary endothelial cells, but not by those flowing in the blood.
source: This discrepancy probably arises from the fact that most of the tumor cells were killed by NK cells crawling on the pulmonary endothelial cells, but not by those flowing in the blood.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing that crawling NK cells account for 77% of Ca2+ influx events.

claim: LFA-1 engagement of ICAM on pulmonary endothelial cells contributes to the pre-activation status of NK cells.
source: Binding of LFA-1 to its ligand ICAM-1 induces reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and polarization of NK cells, which is a prerequisite for subsequent redistribution of cytotoxic granules toward the bound targets (Mace et al., 2009). It is likely that LFA-1 engagement of ICAM on pulmonary endothelial cells contributes to the pre-activation status of NK cells.
evidence: Inferred from the known role of LFA-1 in NK cell activation and the requirement for LFA-1 in tumor elimination.

claim: The slow migration speed of NK cells in the presence of tumor cells may indicate the increased fraction of active NK cells.
source: In this regard, the slow migration speed of NK cells in the presence of tumor cells may indicate the increased fraction of active NK cells (Figure 3).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed decrease in NK cell migration speed.

claim: DNAM-1 expression in NK cells contributes to the rejection of B16F10 melanoma cells.
source: In the B16F10 melanoma metastasis model, DNAM-1 expression in NK cells contributes to the rejection of tumor cells (Gilfillan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Upon target cell engagement, ERK is rapidly activated in DNAM-1+ NK cells, but not DNAM-1− NK cells.
source: In agreement with a previous report (Zhang et al., 2015), we have shown that, upon target cell engagement, ERK is rapidly activated in DNAM-1+ NK cells, but not DNAM-1− NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and citation to previous study.

claim: About 60% of lung NK cells express DNAM-1.
source: Only about 60% of lung NK cells express DNAM-1 (Tahara-Hanaoka et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: DNAM-1 serves as an adhesion molecule.
source: Because DNAM-1 serves as an adhesion molecule (Kim et al., 2017; Shibuya et al., 1996), the crawling NK cells may be biased to DNAM-1+ NK cells, consistent with the potent cytotoxic activity of the crawling cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The crawling NK cells may be biased to DNAM-1+ NK cells.
source: Because DNAM-1 serves as an adhesion molecule (Kim et al., 2017; Shibuya et al., 1996), the crawling NK cells may be biased to DNAM-1+ NK cells, consistent with the potent cytotoxic activity of the crawling cells.
evidence: Inferred from the adhesion function of DNAM-1 and the high cytotoxic activity of crawling NK cells.

claim: The number of lung metastasis was significantly increased in DNAM-1-deficient mice, but markedly less than mice injected with αAGM1.
source: First, Gilfillan et al., 2008 observed that the number of lung metastasis was significantly increased in DNAM-1-deficient mice, but markedly less than mice injected with αAGM1, indicating that DNAM-1-Necl5 interaction is not the only mechanism of B16F10 rejection by NK cells (Gilfillan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: DNAM-1-Necl5 interaction is not the only mechanism of B16F10 rejection by NK cells.
source: First, Gilfillan et al., 2008 observed that the number of lung metastasis was significantly increased in DNAM-1-deficient mice, but markedly less than mice injected with αAGM1, indicating that DNAM-1-Necl5 interaction is not the only mechanism of B16F10 rejection by NK cells (Gilfillan et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DNAM-1 deficiency has less effect than complete NK cell depletion.

claim: Lung metastasis of B16F10 cells was impaired in DNAM-1 deficient mice treated with cytokines.
source: Second, Chan et al., 2010 reported that lung metastasis of B16F10 cells was impaired in DNAM-1 deficient mice treated with cytokines; however, neither DNAM-1 deficiency nor anti-DNAM-1 did not exhibit significant effects on the lung metastasis in the absence of cytokine administration (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Neither DNAM-1 deficiency nor anti-DNAM-1 exhibited significant effects on lung metastasis in the absence of cytokine administration.
source: Second, Chan et al., 2010 reported that lung metastasis of B16F10 cells was impaired in DNAM-1 deficient mice treated with cytokines; however, neither DNAM-1 deficiency nor anti-DNAM-1 did not exhibit significant effects on the lung metastasis in the absence of cytokine administration (Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Necl5 is critical for tumor cell migration and survival.
source: Third, Li et al., 2018 reported that Necl5-deficient B16F10 cells form lung metastasis less efficiently than WT cells because Necl5 is critical for tumor cell migration and survival (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Necl5-deficient B16F10 cells form lung metastasis less efficiently than WT cells.
source: Third, Li et al., 2018 reported that Necl5-deficient B16F10 cells form lung metastasis less efficiently than WT cells because Necl5 is critical for tumor cell migration and survival (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: There are three receptors, DNAM-1, TIGIT, and CD96, that bind to Necl5 with different affinity.
source: Moreover, there are three receptors, DNAM-1, TIGIT, and CD96, that bind to Necl5 with different affinity, 119, 3.15, and 37.6 nM, respectively (Martinet and Smyth, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: TIGIT and CD96 exhibit higher affinity than DNAM-1 for Necl5.
source: Since the two inhibitory receptors, TIGIT and CD96, exhibit higher affinity than the activating receptor DNAM-1, thrombin-mediated reduction of Necl5 may strengthen the inhibitory signal.
evidence: Inferred from the reported binding affinities of the receptors.

claim: Thrombin-mediated reduction of Necl5 may strengthen the inhibitory signal.
source: Since the two inhibitory receptors, TIGIT and CD96, exhibit higher affinity than the activating receptor DNAM-1, thrombin-mediated reduction of Necl5 may strengthen the inhibitory signal.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on receptor affinities.

claim: TIGIT+ NK cells can eliminate Necl5−/− cells in vivo by missing-self recognition due to education via Necl5 on host cells.
source: Finally, the discrepancy could also be explained by the previous reports that TIGIT+ NK cells can eliminate Necl5−/− cells in vivo by missing-self recognition due to the education via Necl5 on the host cells (He et al., 2017) and that the effect of education on degranulation does not last in cell culture with IL2 (Pugh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The effect of education on degranulation does not last in cell culture with IL2.
source: Finally, the discrepancy could also be explained by the previous reports that TIGIT+ NK cells can eliminate Necl5−/− cells in vivo by missing-self recognition due to the education via Necl5 on the host cells (He et al., 2017) and that the effect of education on degranulation does not last in cell culture with IL2 (Pugh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The elimination mechanism of Necl5 and Nectin2 knockout cells is NK cell-dependent but Ca2+ influx-independent.
source: The elimination mechanism of Necl5 and Nectin2 knockout cells is suggested to be NK cell-dependent but Ca2+ influx-independent manners because we did not detect Ca2+ influx in Necl5 and Nectin2 knockout cells in vivo (Figures 4H and 6K).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that knockout cells are eliminated but do not show Ca2+ influx.

claim: Shedding of ligands for the activating receptors of NK cells has been documented for NKG2D.
source: Shedding of ligands for the activating receptors of NK cells has been documented for NKG2D (Raulet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The NKG2D ligands, MICA, MICB, and ULBP2 are cleaved by matrix metalloproteases (MMPs), leading to evasion of NK surveillance.
source: The NKG2D ligands, MICA, MICB, and ULBP2 are cleaved by matrix metalloproteases (MMPs), leading to evasion of NK surveillance.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Raulet et al., 2013).

claim: Platelets can promote the MMP-mediated shedding of the NKG2D ligands in vitro.
source: It is also reported that platelets can promote the MMP-mediated shedding of the NKG2D ligands in vitro (Maurer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Necl5 on tumor cells facilitates adhesion to the lung capillary but also invokes NK cell attack.
source: Interestingly, Necl5 contributes to cell adhesion as does DNAM-1 (Takai et al., 2008). Therefore, Necl5 on tumor cells is a double-edge sword, which facilitates adhesion to the lung capillary but also invokes NK cell attack.
evidence: Inferred from the dual role of Necl5 in adhesion and NK cell activation.

claim: After anchoring to the capillaries, tumor cells take advantage of thrombin's capacity to strip Necl5 from the cell surface within 24 hr after adhesion.
source: To evade the NK cell surveillance, after anchoring to the capillaries, tumor cells are able to take advantage of the capacity of thrombin to strip Necl5 from the cell surface within 24 hr after adhesion (Figure 6J).
evidence: Inferred from the observed loss of Necl5 and the effect of thrombin inhibition.

claim: A higher number of circulating or tumor-infiltrating NK cells is correlated with better patient outcomes in human patients.
source: In human patients, a higher number of circulating or tumor-infiltrating NK cells is correlated with better patient outcomes (López-Soto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Selective depletion of NK cells markedly increases the metastatic burden in immunocompetent mice.
source: In immunocompetent mice, selective depletion of NK cells markedly increases the metastatic burden (Diefenbach et al., 2001; Smyth et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.
